questions.q: For the Bell state's seeded draw {'00': 503, '11': 521, '01': 0, '10': 0}, what does plot_histogram actually render?
options: Four bars of equal height
Two bars, for 00 and 11, near mid-height, with no bars at all for 01 or 10
A single bar averaging all four outcomes
A pie chart, not a bar chart
questions.explain: Only 00 and 11 have nonzero counts (503 and 521 of 1024), so only those two bars appear; 01 and 10 are absent from the chart entirely, not shown at zero height.

questions.q: Why is a per-qubit Bloch sphere misleading when applied to one qubit of the entangled Bell state?
options: It isn't misleading — it works exactly the same as for an unentangled qubit

Because that qubit's individual reduced state is maximally mixed, sitting at the center of the sphere rather than at a point on its surface, so there's no definite single-qubit state to point an arrow at
Because Qiskit refuses to render it at all
Because the Bloch sphere only works for 3+ qubits
questions.explain: An entangled qubit's own reduced state has 50/50 outcome probability with no definite phase to point to — geometrically a maximally mixed state sits at the Bloch sphere's center, not on its surface, making a per-qubit Bloch plot of an entangled state fundamentally uninformative.

questions.q: What does plot_state_qsphere show for the Bell state that plot_bloch_multivector (applied per-qubit) cannot?
options: Nothing different — they show the same information
The actual entanglement structure: two equal-size, equal-color blobs at 00 and 11, directly showing which basis states participate and their relative phase
The number of shots run
The hardware backend name
questions.explain: The Q-sphere operates on the joint 2-qubit statevector and shows the real amplitude/phase structure (two equal blobs at 00 and 11), information that simply isn't present in either qubit's individually meaningless per-qubit Bloch picture.

questions.q: For a non-technical stakeholder asking "did the quantum computer do what we expected?", which visualization is the best fit, and why?
options: The Q-sphere, because it looks the most impressive
The histogram, because it maps directly onto a question about measured outcomes without requiring any background in phase or superposition
The Bloch sphere, because spheres are intuitive to everyone
State-city, because it has the most bars
questions.explain: The histogram answers exactly the question a non-technical stakeholder is asking — what outcomes came out and how often — without requiring an explanation of amplitudes or relative phase first.

questions.q: A colleague's circuit has a bug that flips a relative phase between 00 and 11 but leaves the measurement probabilities (0.5/0.5) unchanged. Which visualization would reveal the bug, and which would miss it entirely?
options: The histogram would reveal it; the Q-sphere would miss it
The Q-sphere would reveal it (via a color/phase difference on the blobs); the histogram would miss it entirely, since measurement destroys phase information
Both would reveal it equally well
Neither visualization could ever reveal a phase bug
questions.explain: Measurement collapses phase information, so the histogram looks identical whether or not the relative phase is flipped. The Q-sphere encodes relative phase directly as blob color, so a phase flip would show up as a visible color change even though the probabilities (blob sizes) stay the same.
